input: Stock a three-day emergency preparedness kit at home

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The number of adults, children, elderly, or pets in the household directly determines quantities of food, water, medications, and other supplies needed.

Emergency kits can range from basic survival (water, food, first aid) to comprehensive setups (sanitation, power, communications, documents). Knowing what is already owned vs. what needs to be acquired shapes the full shopping and assembly list.
The most likely local hazards — earthquake, hurricane, wildfire, power outage, flooding — change which specific items are prioritized (e.g., dust masks vs. life jackets vs. warm blankets).
A strict budget determines whether to buy a pre-built kit, build one piece by piece over time, or source items from what is already at home.
Available storage space and container type (one grab-and-go bag vs. a dedicated shelf) affect how the kit is organized and whether it needs to be portable or can be stationary.
Knowing the target completion date — e.g., fully stocked by a specific week — determines whether this is a single focused shopping trip or a phased build-out plan.
Special dietary needs, medical conditions, or allergies among household members change which food, water, and medical items must be included or substituted.

gold.taskTitle: Stock a three-day home emergency preparedness kit
gold.taskDescription: Assemble and store a complete 72-hour emergency kit at home, covering supplies for survival, safety, and self-sufficiency during a disaster or crisis.

questions.title: How many people and pets need to be covered?
questions.description: Identify the total number of household members — adults, children, elderly — and any pets, as this drives all quantity calculations for food, water, and supplies.

questions.title: Which disaster types are most likely in your area?
questions.description: Determine the primary local hazards (e.g., earthquake, hurricane, wildfire, severe winter storm, flooding) to prioritize the right category of supplies.

questions.title: What supplies do you already have at home?
questions.description: Establish a baseline of existing items — first aid kit, flashlights, stored water, canned food — to avoid duplicate purchases and identify true gaps.

questions.title: What is your total budget for building this kit?
questions.description: A defined spending limit shapes whether to buy a pre-assembled kit, prioritize essentials first, or phase purchases across several weeks.

questions.title: Does anyone in your household have special dietary or medical needs?
questions.description: Capture allergies, prescription medications, mobility aids, infant formula, or other personal health requirements that must be reflected in the kit contents.

questions.title: Should the kit be portable, stationary, or both?
questions.description: Decide whether the kit should be a single grab-and-go bag for evacuation, a fixed home stockpile, or a combination — this determines containers, storage location, and organization.

questions.title: By when do you want the kit fully stocked?
questions.description: Set a target completion date to determine whether this is a single focused effort or a multi-week phased plan with milestones.
